title: What is biospeleology?
summary: Josh and Chuck record inside a cave to explain biospeleology, the study of life in caves, distinguishing it from speleology (cave research) and spelunking (recreational caving). They cover the history of discovery in the 1700s, the Proteus salamander (olm) with no eyes and pigmentation, regressive evolution, and the three classes of cave fauna: trogloxenes (visitors), troglophiles (cave lovers), and troglobites (cave-only species). They describe the entrance, twilight, and dark zones, how food reaches deep caves via flooding and bat guano, and the decomposer-based food pyramid. They discuss human threats such as contamination, the Federal Cave Resources Protection Act, climate change, and white-nose syndrome in bats. The episode closes with listener-mail-style housekeeping: a trivia event in Atlanta, a tour, fundraising for Guatemala and Haiti-related campaigns, and social media plugs.
topics: Stuff You Should Know live trivia

segments.title: Opening banter in a cave
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode from inside a cave, defining biospeleology versus speleology and spelunking, and joke about faceless creatures and aliens.

segments.title: Cave life and the Proteus salamander
segments.summary: Cave life was only studied from the 1700s on. The Proteus salamander, a foot-long eyeless, pigmentless cave salamander, is discussed, along with cave shrimp and other cave animals descended from surface species.

segments.title: Regressive evolution in caves
segments.summary: Regressive evolution is explained as losing features like eyes and pigment to suit darkness. Cave organisms have efficient, hypermetabolic systems because food is scarce, and studying them informs human medicine and water quality research.

segments.title: Trogloxenes, troglophiles, and troglobites
segments.summary: The three categories of cave fauna are defined by how much time they spend in caves: trogloxenes are visitors such as bats and bears, troglophiles live in and out of caves such as beetles and frogs, and troglobites never leave and show adaptations like no eyes and long antennae.

segments.title: Entrance, twilight, and dark zones
segments.summary: The three cave zones are described: the sunlit entrance zone, the twilight zone with fungi and moisture, and the dark zone with no light, stable temperature, and no vegetation. Food reaches the dark zone through flooding and a food chain, and The Descent is mentioned.

segments.title: Bat guano, decomposers, and the cave food pyramid
segments.summary: Bat guano feeds decomposer microorganisms, which feed small insects, then larger predators such as centipedes, which can eat bats. Human activity like shedding lint can disrupt these fragile ecosystems.

segments.title: Threats to caves: contamination, law, climate, white-nose syndrome
segments.summary: Cave ecosystems are described as nearly pristine and vulnerable to introduced fungi and bacteria. The Federal Cave Resources Protection Act is mentioned, climate change threatens stable cave temperatures, and white-nose syndrome is killing bat populations, which matters because bats eat mosquitoes.

segments.title: Listener mail and housekeeping
segments.summary: Hosts announce an Atlanta trivia event, a tour, social media channels, and fundraising campaigns, then sign off with contact info.
